name: lines-1

lines.text: Start here. Money only ever does two things. It comes in to you, and it goes out from you. That's it. Get a grip on both and you're already ahead of most people. No experience needed. We'll teach every word as we go.
Money that comes in to you is called income.
Money that goes out to pay for something is an expense.
Take your expenses away from your income and you get your cash flow: what’s left over. Earn $2,000, spend $1,500, and your cash flow is $500.
When income is bigger than expenses, cash flow is positive. When expenses are bigger, it's negative: you're spending money you don't have.
Here’s your first pay stub from a coffee shop job. Your gross pay is everything you earned, before anything is taken out.
Money taken out of your pay before you get it is a deduction. Taxes are deductions. So is money you choose to save for retirement.
What’s left after every deduction is your take-home pay, also called net pay. It’s the number that actually lands in your account.
Not every deduction is a tax. Some of it is still your money, just saved for later.
Some expenses cost exactly the same every month, like rent. Those are fixed expenses.
Other expenses go up and down depending on what you do, like food or fuel. Those are variable expenses.
Add both kinds together to get your total spending. Fixed $1,000 plus variable $500 equals $1,500 a month.
A need is something you have to pay for to live and work: a place to live, basic food, getting to your job.
A want is something that makes life nicer, but you'd be fine without it.
Careful: wants love to hide inside needs. Food is a need, but takeout every night is a want.
When people start earning more, they often spend more on wants without noticing. That's called lifestyle creep.

name: lines-2

lines.text: Groceries are a need. But a want can still sneak into the basket.
Planning a month before it starts beats wondering where it went.
An asset is something you own that's worth money: savings in the bank, a car, a laptop you could sell.
A liability is money you owe to someone else, like a loan you're still paying back.
Your net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. Own $10,000, owe $4,000, and your net worth is $6,000.
Net worth can drop below zero. If you owe more than you own, it's negative. That's common when you're starting out. What matters is that it grows.
Every bill has a due date: the last day to pay it without being late.
Pay after the due date and many companies add a late fee: a penalty for paying late. Read the small print at the bottom.
Read the lines, not just the total. Mistakes and surprise charges hide in there.
Comparing two prices? Line them up over the same stretch of time, like a full year.

name: mf-jordan-story

lines.text: Where did it all go? Jordan just moved into a first apartment and started a full-time job. Every month, $2,400 of take-home pay lands in Jordan’s account. Rent is $1,100. Phone and internet are $100. Groceries come to about $300. This month Jordan also spent $420 eating out and $180 on two concerts, and put $0 into savings. At the end of the month Jordan opens the bank app and wonders where it all went.

name: mf-snapshot-story

lines.text: A one-page check-up Maya sat down to see where she stands. Each month she takes home $3,200. Her expenses: rent $1,300, groceries $350, a car payment of $280, her phone $60, and about $700 on eating out and shopping. She owns a car worth $9,000 and has $2,500 in the bank. She still owes $6,000 on the car and $1,200 to a friend.
